abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Immunotherapy, encompassing immune checkpoint inhibitors, antibody therapy, and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T-cell therapy, has emerged as a groundbreaking approach by harnessing the immune system to selectively target and eliminate malignant cells. However, its widespread application has revealed a spectrum of severe, life-threatening hemostatic abnormalities, including immune thrombocytopenia, Evans syndrome, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, acquired haemophilia A, thrombosis, disseminated intravascular coagulation and CAR-T-associated coagulopathy. These disorders may arise from excessive immune activation, autoantibody production, and intricate crosstalk between inflammatory pathways and coagulation cascades. Despite increasing recognition, their pathophysiological mechanisms remain incompletely understood, and standardized management strategies have yet to be established, posing significant clinical challenges. Given the safety concerns surrounding immunotherapy, timely diagnosis and appropriate intervention of these abnormalities are crucial. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the epidemiology, distinct clinical manifestations, emerging pathophysiological insights, and evolving treatment paradigms of immunotherapy-associated hemostatic abnormalities to enhance clinicians’ understanding and guide therapeutic decision-making.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: In recent decades, immunotherapy has significantly transformed the landscape of cancer treatment, encompassing a range of modalities, such as immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T-cell therapy, bispecific antibodies (BsAbs), cytokine therapy, oncolytic viruses, and tumour vaccines [1, 2]. These advancements have led to notable improvements in the response rates and overall survival outcomes for cancer patients [2]. As of 2024, a total of nineteen ICIs, ten CAR-T-cell products and thirteen BsAbs have been approved globally (Table 1) [3, 4].

sec.p: The fundamental principle of immunotherapy lies in modulating the host immune system to bolster its efficacy in combating cancer. This characteristic, however, may result in distinct immune-related adverse events (irAEs) [5]. Patients receiving ICIs treatment commonly experience irAEs such as lung, liver, endocrine, and skin toxicities [6]. In patients receiving CAR-T-cell therapy, cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) are frequently observed [7]. The predominant irAEs linked to BsAbs include pyrexia, fatigue, infection, cytopenia and CRS [8]. With the widespread implementation of immunotherapy in clinical practice, increasing reports of immunotherapy-associated hemostatic abnormalities have been documented [9–12]. For ICI- and BsAb-associated hemostatic abnormalities, slightly abnormal coagulation indicators are often present without clinical manifestations, which indicates a potential underestimation and miscalculation of the incidence. Studies based on isolated case reports and case series have investigated various hemostatic abnormalities, including immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), Evans syndrome, immune-mediated thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (iTTP), acquired haemophilia A (AHA), thrombosis and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) [9, 13–15]. Timely identification and appropriate management are crucial to prevent potentially fatal outcomes. These complications, which have also been observed in patients receiving CAR-T-cell therapy, are referred to as CAR-T-cell-associated coagulopathy (CARAC) by Mei et al. [16]. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the field of immunotherapy-associated hemostatic abnormalities, including its epidemiology, pathological mechanisms and clinical management principles.

sec.title: ITP
sec.p: ITP, which is the most commonly observed haematological complication during ICIs therapy, is an acquired autoimmune haemorrhagic disorder characterized by an unexplained decrease in the platelet count [17]. The incidence of ITP in patients receiving ICIs therapy (approximately 0.47%) is significantly higher than that in the general population (approximately 2–5 per 100000 individuals) [17, 18]. The mortality rate of ICI-associated ITP is approximately 11–31% [15, 19, 20]. In a meta-analysis performed by Wilson et al., ITP accounted for 27% (36/135) of haematological irAEs [21]. According to a study on Vigibase, the World Health Organization’s pharmacovigilance database of individual case safety reports, from 2010 to 2018, ITP accounted for 40% (68/168) of haematological complications related to ICIs (Table 2) [15]. Moreover, in a real-world study of the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) adverse event reporting system database (FAERS) conducted by Bai et al., the risk of ITP in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients following treatment with a combination of a programmed death (-ligand) protein 1 (PD-(L)1) inhibitor and bevacizumab was 5.5 times greater than that after anti-PD-(L)1 monotherapy [19]. The median onset time of ICI-associated ITP was 44 days (range: 1–1368 days), indicating that ITP can occur at various time points, from the beginning of treatment to several months after ICIs treatment [20]. Most observed cases are Grade 2–4 ITP [15, 22]. The main manifestation of ITP is a decreased platelet count (platelets < 100 × 109/L). Approximately 10% of ITP cases involve bleeding events, such as mucosal bleeding (gingival or nasal bleeding), petechiae (often in the lower limbs), and gastrointestinal haemorrhage [18, 20]. In severe cases, cerebral haemorrhage and subarachnoid haemorrhage may occur, with platelet counts decreasing to < 5 × 109/L, the immature platelet fraction increasing to 15.4%, and an elevated number of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow [18, 23].

sec.p: The pathogenesis of primary ITP involves the decreased production and excessive destruction of platelets [43]. However, ICIs therapy may aggravate this pathological process because of its ability to enhance the activity of the immune system [24, 44, 45]. Because cytotoxic T-lymphocyteassociated protein (CTLA)−4 and PD-1 are crucial for the immunosuppressive function and proliferation of Tregs, patients receiving CTLA-4 or PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors exhibit Treg dysfunction and the activation of CD4+ helper T cells and CD8+ cytotoxic T cells. These conditions eventually lead to the disordered differentiation of haematopoietic stem cells and disrupted maturation of megakaryocytes [46–49]. Moreover, PD-1 inhibitors can induce the activation of B cells and increase the secretion of autoantibodies, especially when PD-1 expression is upregulated on the B-cell surface (Fig. 1) [24, 43, 44]. In addition, the presence of other autoantibodies (such as antinuclear antibodies, anticardiolipin antibodies, and/or rheumatoid factors) and certain single nucleotide polymorphisms in PD-1 and CTLA-4 can increase the risk of ITP [24–26, 50].

caption.p: Potential mechanisms of immunotherapy-associated hemostatic abnormalities (a) ITP: The activation of T cells and inflammatory pathways damage haematopoietic stem cells and reduce the production of PLTs; The production of antiplatelet antibodies leads to the excessive PLTs destruction, driven by B cell activation and decreased immunosuppression due to Treg depletion or dysfunction after ICI therapy. (b) VTE: Increased numbers of MDSCs and proinflammatory factors such as IL-8 are observed before ICI treatment, the activation of immune cells and cytokine release induced by ICIs may enhance the prethrombotic state by activating the coagulation system and platelets and releasing NETs. (c) ATE: ICIs enhance pro-atherogenic T cell responses and induce the production of inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IFN-γ; These cytokines activate macrophages, promote their transformation into foam cells, and contribute to the formation of necrotic cores, thereby destabilizing AS plaques and accelerating AS progression; plaque rupture triggers platelet activation and aggregation, thrombus formation, and ultimately leading to ATE. (d) DIC:Tumor cell rupture, release of tissue factor and proinflammatory/procoagulant mediators, PD-L1 overexpression, ICI-induced immune overactivation, and cytokine storms can collectively trigger coagulation activation and lead to DIC. (e) CARAC: CRS after CAR-T-cell interaction with tumour cells and activation of macrophages can cause endothelial injury, coagulation and fibrinolysis activation; the release of HMGB-1 and histones due to tumour lysis and the off-target effects of CAR-T cells, which can damage hepatocytes, may also exacerbate CARAC. sec.p: As specific diagnostic guidelines for ICI-associated ITP are currently unavailable, the diagnostic criteria for primary ITP can be applied [17, 23, 51]. The diagnosis of ICI-associated ITP is exclusionary and should be considered in the presence of unexplained thrombocytopenia and bleeding symptoms following ICIs treatment [17, 22, 23, 51]. According to the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) guidelines, ICI therapy can be administered when ITP occurs [23]. However, if the platelet count is < 75 × 109/L and does not recover after monitoring, ICIs therapy should be discontinued in patients with solid tumours [23]. This approach may not be applicable for patients with haematological malignancies because of the influence of the tumour itself on the haematopoietic system. Corticosteroids remain the first-line treatment for ICI-associated ITP, and the response rate is 50–86% [21–23]. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) may be used in conjunction with corticosteroids if a more rapid increase in the platelet count is needed [23]. Rituximab, thrombopoietin receptor agonists, or more potent immunosuppression may be considered when previous treatment with corticosteroids and/or IVIG fails [23]. The response rate for rituximab as second-line treatment is approximately 60% [21, 22]. Patients with ICI-associated ITP who are rechallenged with ICIs may experience ITP relapse, but this finding is still inconclusive [20].

sec.title: Other bleeding and thrombosis complications meditated by autoantibody
sec.p: Owing to the extensive activation of T and B cells and weakened immunosuppressive function of Tregs induced by ICI therapy, the generation of autoantibodies contributes to other hemostatic abnormalities, such as Evans syndrome, iTTP, and AHA [52–54].

sec.title: Evans syndrome
sec.p: Evans syndrome is a rare condition characterized by the concomitant or subsequent presence of ITP, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA), and autoimmune neutropenia [55]. The estimated incidence is 1–9 cases per million people per year, and few cases associated with ICIs have been reported [52, 55, 56]. The clinical manifestations of ICI-associated Evans syndrome include petechial purpura and deep vein thrombosis. Laboratory tests, such as direct and indirect Coombs tests, typically yield positive results, and platelet-associated IgG antibodies are often detected [52, 56]. To date, prednisone remains an effective treatment with a favourable response [55]. 71% of ITP patients and 78% of AIHA patients respond well to steroids [22]. In addition, according to the first consensus recommendations for Evans syndrome in adults, rituximab, thrombopoietin receptor agonists, and fostamatinib can be used in certain conditions [55].

sec.title: iTTP
sec.p: iTTP is a life-threatening autoimmune complication associated with ICIs that is highlighted by the presence of autoantibodies against ADAMTS13 (a disintegrin and metalloproteinase with a thrombospondin type 1 motif, member 13) [57]. According to a retrospective observational analysis of FAERS data between 2011 and 2021, 35 cases of ICI-induced TTP among 18,055,043 adverse events have been reported [57]. Nivolumab-induced TTP accounts for approximately 51% of these cases, among which 39% involve concomitant ipilimumab use [57]. In addition, iTTP can also occur during treatment with pembrolizumab, atezolizumab, or durvalumab [57]. However, as the FAERS is a spontaneous case reporting system, reporting bias exists, and the true incidence of complications cannot be determined. The median onset time of iTTP is after 3 treatment cycles (ranging from 1 to 7 cycles) [57]. Patients with ICI-induced TTP may exhibit symptoms such as fever, mild renal failure, thrombocytopenia, and neurologic manifestations such as seizures, hemiplegia, and visual disturbances [23, 53]. The presence of ADAMTS13 antibodies inhibits the proteolytic activity of ADAMTS13 on large von Willebrand factor multimers. This contributes to endothelial injury, platelet adhesion and consumption, and the development of microvascular haemolytic anaemia due to increased shear stress [53, 57]. Early identification and monitoring of ICI-induced TTP are critical, as delays in diagnosis are associated with increased mortality, with 23% of reported cases being fatal [23, 57]. Plasma exchange and corticosteroids are the primary treatments for ICI-induced TTP. When ADAMTS13 inhibitors are detected or ADAMTS13 activity is < 10% of the normal activity, rituximab or the anti- von Willebrand factor nanobody caplacizumab should be considered [23, 53, 57]. Patients experiencing ICI-induced TTP should have their ICI therapy held [23]. To our knowledge, no case studies support to rechallenge with ICI therapy following TTP, considering the life-threatening nature of this condition.

sec.title: AHA
sec.p: Twelve unique reports of AHA associated with ICIs, including nivolumab (n = 7), ipilimumab (n = 3), pembrolizumab (n = 3), and a combination of nivolumab and ipilimumab (n = 1), were identified in the FAERS database from 2001 to 2021 [58]. Among the reported ICI-induced AHA cases, two deaths involving treatment with pembrolizumab and ipilimumab have been reported [58]. ICI-induced AHA usually presents at a median of 7.5 weeks (range: 3 weeks to 17 months) and is characterized by spontaneous subcutaneous haemorrhage, soft tissue and joint haemorrhage, macroscopic haematuria, and extensive bruising [54, 58, 59]. Laboratory findings include a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time following ICI treatment, decreased coagulation factor VIII (FVIII) activity, and the presence of FVIII antibodies, which are major contributors [54, 58, 59]. The therapeutic strategy for ICI-induced AHA focuses on promptly controlling bleeding and eradicating autoantibodies while continuing ICI therapy. The recommended treatments include transfusion support and the administration of prednisone, rituximab, and cyclophosphamide, with the choice of therapy based on the AHA severity [23, 58].

sec.title: Venous Thromboembolism (VTE)
sec.p: The incidence of ICI-associated thrombosis is relatively higher than that of other ICI-associated hemostatic abnormalities. A large population-based cohort study revealed that the 6-month risk of VTE was 12 times higher in cancer patients than in the general population, 24.4 times higher in patients receiving chemotherapy, and 71 times higher in patients receiving immunotherapy [60]. Several systematic studies have reported that the incidence of VTE associated with ICIs ranges from 2.7 to 24% [10, 27, 28]. The cumulative incidence of VTE increases over time, with rates of 2.4% at 3 months, 5–8% at 6 months, 7–13.8% at 12 months and 9% at 24 months (Table 2) [10, 13, 27, 29, 30]. The risk of VTE is comparable among different ICIs, such as nivolumab, pembrolizumab, ipilimumab, and atezolizumab, with an 8.5-month cumulative incidence ranging from 9.8 to 19.9% [13]. Notably, the cumulative incidence was higher in patients receiving combination ICIs therapy compared to those treated with a single agent (16.7% vs. 5.0% at 6 months; 21.3% vs. 9.5% at 12 months) [28]. The most common types of VTE include deep vein thrombosis (36.2–46%), pulmonary embolism (3.2–38.3%) and isceral vein thrombosis (5.4–10.6%) [10, 13, 27, 28, 31]. Two-thirds of thrombosis occur after 6 months of ICI therapy, unlike chemotherapy-associated thrombosis, which typically occurs within 6 months [61]. This difference may be due to the significant therapeutic benefits and prolonged survival associated with ICIs, as such treatment extends both the exposure to ICIs and the risk of thrombosis-related factors.

Currently, no conclusive evidence regarding the risk factors for ICI-associated VTE is available. Moik et al. conducted a single-centre retrospective cohort study of 672 patients who received ICI therapy [13]. The occurrence of ICI-associated VTE was related to a prior history of VTE but not to the tumour type and stage, PD-L1 expression level, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group score, Khorana score, or Chilson comorbidity index [13]. In contrast, in a multivariate analysis of a retrospective cohort study involving 1686 patients receiving ICIs, Roopkumar et al. reported that metastatic disease was significantly associated with VTE [10]. Sussman et al. found that combination ICI, Khorana Score ≥ 1, history of coronary artery disease, and anticoagulation at treatment start were risk factors significantly associated with VTE by multivariate analysis [28]. A retrospective multicentric cohort study involving 593 patients with NSCLC revealed that an age younger than 65 years and tumours exhibiting PD-L1 levels ≥ 1% were associated with a higher risk of VTE during ICI therapy [62]. The limitations of the current retrospective study may lead to bias in the results, such as different study designs and inclusion criteria and the inconsistent inclusion of indicators that are not available for all patients. In the future, large comparative cohort analyses, standardized examinations of thrombi and rigorous follow-ups are needed. Inflammatory biomarkers may play crucial roles in the biomarker-based VTE risk prediction. Following ICIs treatment, the cumulative incidence of VTE in patients whose C reactive protein (CRP) levels increased by more than 2.5 times within 3 months was significantly higher than that in the control group (17.5% vs. 2.9%) [63]. In addition, elevated levels of myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), interleukin (IL)−8, and soluble vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 prior to immunotherapy are correlated with the development of VTE [10].

Several similarities in the mechanisms of ICI- and chemotherapy-induced VTE have been noted, both of which involve inflammatory factors and the overactivation of coagulation. Several potential mechanisms have been proposed based on previous studies (Fig. 1). (1) ICIs induce immune cell activation and cytokine release, leading to systemic proinflammatory stimulation, which in turn enhances the prethrombotic state by activating the coagulation system and inhibiting fibrinolysis [64]. (2) Elevated levels of MDSCs and proinflammatory factors such as IL-8 in peripheral blood prior to treatment induce platelet activation and the release of neutrophil extracellular traps, increasing the risk of ICI-associated VTE [10, 65]. (3) Additional factors may include the failure of previous treatments, advanced disease, and other thrombosis risk factors, such as NSCLC and other tumour cancer types with a high risk of tumour-associated VTE [66, 67].

According to the ASCO guidelines for ICI-related adverse events, the primary management strategy is to treat VTE events, prevent complications such as pulmonary embolism, avoid immunosuppressive therapy, and continue ICI treatment in the absence of other irAEs when the patient is stable [23]. Anticoagulants are currently recommended as a prophylactic measure for cancer patients with high susceptibility (Khorana ≥ 2) to thrombosis before starting a new systemic regimen [23]. Apixaban, rivaroxaban, or low-molecular-weight heparin can be used for thromboprophylaxis, provided that the patient has no significant bleeding risks or drug interactions [68]. However, the benefit of primary thromboprophylaxis in patients receiving ICIs remains investigational, as the Khorana score, which is designed for chemotherapy patients, may not accurately assess the VTE risk in patients receiving ICIs [68, 69]. For initial anticoagulation, low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH), vitamin K agonists (VKAs), dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban, or edoxaban can be considered. Intravenous heparin is an acceptable alternative for initial use [13, 23]. For long-term anticoagulation, treatment with LMWH, edoxaban, rivaroxaban, or apixaban for at least 6 months is preferred over VKA therapy because of the improved efficacy [13, 23]. Anticoagulant therapy should be continued until six months after the completion of ICI treatment [13, 23]. The choice of anticoagulants should depend on the characteristics of the patient and tumour, bleeding risk, patient preference, and affordability [29, 68, 70]. Clinicians should carefully evaluate the risks and benefits to determine whether to continue immunotherapy [13, 23].

sec.title: Arterial Thromboembolism (ATE)
sec.p: The incidence of ATE in patients receiving ICIs is relatively lower than ATE, ranging from 1.1 to 6.1% [27, 28]. The cumulative incidence rates are 0.6% at 3 months, 1–2.2% at 6 months, 1–5% at 12 months and 1.8% at 24 months (Table 2) [13, 27, 29, 30]. Notably, the risk of ATE appears comparable between combination and single-agent ICI therapy at both 6 and 12 months [28]. Clinically, ATE typically presents as acute coronary syndrome, myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, acute vascular occlusion, or transient ischemic attack [13, 27, 31]. Several studies have identified potential risk factors associated with ICI- associated ATE. In a retrospective cohort analysis by Zhu et al., the incidence of ATE increased with longer ICI treatment duration, particularly beyond one year. Advanced age, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, peripheral atherosclerosis, atrial fibrillation, chronic ischemic heart disease, distant metastases, and prolonged ICI exposure were all associated with elevated ATE risk [32]. Similarly, Song et al. reported that a high Khorana Risk Score (≥ 3) correlated with an increased incidence of ATE, particularly ischemic stroke, and was also predictive of worse overall survival in ICI-treated patients [33]. PD-L1 inhibitors have been implicated in a higher frequency of ATE events compared to other ICIs [71]. A pooled analysis of 83 randomized clinical trials further suggested that durvalumab may be associated with a relatively higher risk of ATE among single-agent ICIs [72]. The pathophysiology of ICI-associated ATE remains incompletely understood. In general, arterial thrombosis is initiated by rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque, leading to platelet activation, aggregation, and subsequent thrombin generation through the coagulation cascade [73]. ICI-induced immune modulation may contribute to these pathogenic changes. Preclinical studies suggest that ICI therapy may accelerate plaque progression, promote instability, and increase the likelihood of rupture [74, 75]. Specifically, PD-1 inhibitor has been shown to enhance proatherogenic T cell responses, thereby increasing susceptibility to atherosclerosis and thrombosis in murine models [76, 77]. Furthermore, the systemic inflammatory response driven by ICIs may foster a thrombogenic state, compromise vascular endothelial function, and precipitate immune-related cardiotoxicities, collectively amplifying the risk of arterial thrombosis [78].

The management of ATE during ICI therapy remains challenging, as specific preventive and therapeutic strategies have not been established. In clinical practice, treatment is generally based on guidelines for non-cancer populations, including antiplatelet therapy with or without anticoagulation, and risk factor control (e.g., hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, smoking) [29, 79]. A comprehensive cardiovascular risk assessment is recommended prior to initiating ICIs, covering personal and family history, lifestyle factors, blood pressure, lipid profile, and glucose levels [79]. Cardiovascular and cerebrovascular status should be monitored regularly during treatment, and any symptoms such as chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, or neurological deficits should prompt immediate evaluation [79]. Early recognition and timely initiation of antithrombotic therapy are essential. However, the bleeding risk associated with antiplatelet or anticoagulant use must be carefully weighed against the potential benefits. In severe cases, temporary or permanent discontinuation of ICIs may be warranted based on risk–benefit assessment. Given the immune-mediated nature of ICI-related ATE, individualized treatment decisions and multidisciplinary collaboration are crucial.

sec.title: DIC
sec.p: DIC is a fatal thrombohaemorrhagic syndrome that occurs secondary to infectious diseases, trauma, and tumours [80]. DIC has also been reported in patients receiving ICI immunotherapy [81, 82]. In a retrospective study by Ryo et al., among 83 patients with NSCLC, 10 (12%) experienced complications related to coagulation‒fibrinolytic system disorders (thromboembolism or bleeding), primarily occurring in the early stages of ICI treatment and more frequently in patients with high expression of PD-L1 [34]. Among patients with coagulation–fibrinolytic system disorders, 33% (4/12) had ≥ Grade 3 complications according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events, version 5.0, and 82% of cases were strongly correlated with high PD-L1 expression on tumour cells. Furthermore, 72% of patients respond to ICIs [34]. The median onset time of DIC was within one cycle of ICI therapy, and most cases occurred within two cycles [34].

Immune checkpoint blockade activates the immune system and disrupts the coagulation‒fibrinolysis balance. In vitro experiments have shown that activated T cells stimulate antigen-presenting cells, such as monocytes, which subsequently overexpress PD-L1 and tissue factor (TF), initiating coagulation cascades [34]. Additionally, high PD-L1 and TF expression on tumour cells, along with tumour lysis syndrome, further contribute to the pathogenesis of DIC (Fig. 1) [34, 83, 84]. However, the specific mechanisms underlying ICI-related DIC remain poorly understood [34, 81].

The diagnosis of ICI-related DIC is challenging because the clinical manifestations of DIC may overlap with those of the primary disease, making it difficult to distinguish. In addition, distinguishing whether DIC is secondary to a tumour, infection or other causes is necessary. Based on a few case reports, ICI-related DIC can be diagnosed according to the International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis guidelines, Japanese Society of Thrombosis and Hemostasis DIC guidelines, or the Chinese DIC scoring system [85–87]. At present, no specific clinical management for ICI-related DIC is available. The management of ICI-related DIC can use the same approach as general DIC treatment, including a timely aetiological investigation and infusion of platelet suspensions or fresh frozen plasma. Other therapies, such as antithrombin or thrombomodulin, may be considered, depending on the laboratory results and clinical manifestations [80]. Published case studies confirm that patients can recover from immunotherapy-related DIC with prompt and active treatment [81, 82, 87, 88].

sec.title: CARAC
sec.p: CARAC is a clinical syndrome related to CRS that manifests within 28 days after CAR-T-cell infusion and has a relatively high incidence (~ 56%) [11, 16]. CARAC typically presents as bleeding and/or thrombosis, accompanied by a decreased platelet count and abnormal coagulation indicators [11, 16, 35–37]. Clinically significant bleeding events, including gastrointestinal bleeding, extensive maxillofacial bleeding, intracranial bleeding, respiratory haemorrhage, epistaxis, bruising, petechiae, and purpura, occur in 19.6–30% of cases, with most cases categorized as < Grade 3 bleeding events [11, 37, 89]. The cumulative incidence of bleeding within one month is approximately 32.8% [90]. The incidence of thrombosis, including pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis, thrombotic stroke, and visceral vein thrombosis, is relatively low at approximately 6.3–11%, with a median onset time of 20–29 days after CAR-T-cell therapy [35, 36, 91]. A total of 14–50% of CARAC patients develop DIC, mainly patients with Grade ≥ 3 CRS, with a mortality rate ranging from 6.7 to 42.9% [11, 37]. The tumour burden, previous treatment lines, low baseline platelet levels, and particularly the severity of CRS are risk factors for CARAC [11, 37, 38]. In addition, Grade ≥ 3 ICANS is also linked to increased risks of bleeding, thrombosis, and abnormal coagulation indicators (Table 2) [35].

The abnormal laboratory findings in patients with CARAC include abnormal coagulation indicators, endothelial activation, and inflammatory biomarkers (Table 3). Among these indicators, a decreased platelet count and hypofibrinogenemia are the most indicative of coagulation disorders [11, 37, 38, 92]. The endothelial activation and stress index (EASIX) score, defined as lactic dehydrogenase (U/L) × creatinine (mg/dL)/platelets (×109/L), is commonly used to assess endothelial activation and damage in patients who underwent allogeneic transplantation and those with acute graft-versus-host disease. Recent studies have adapted the EASIX to predict coagulopathy after CAR-T-cell therapy [93]. Eugenio Galli et al. proposed a modified EASIX (mEASIX) version, substituting CRP for creatinine. The baseline mEASIX (before lymphodepletion) predicts consumptive coagulopathy and DIC after CAR-T-cell therapy [94]. Wang et al. showed that IL-10 levels plus the EASIX score served as a significant risk factor for bleeding events and effectively established a risk stratification for bleeding events [90].

sec.p: The pathogenesis of CARAC remains unclear, but researchers have speculated that CRS may disrupt the balance between coagulation and fibrinolysis (Fig. 1). CRS can damage vascular endothelial cells, promote the release of TF, expose collagen, and activate extrinsic and intrinsic coagulation pathways [80]. The overexpression of thrombin can subsequently induce further cytokine production, resulting in a vicious cycle of inflammation and coagulation. The serum levels of von Willebrand factor, angiopoietin-2, platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule-1, TF, FXII and P-selectin are significantly higher in patients with severe CRS than in those with mild CRS [11, 38, 95]. In addition, CARAC may be associated with tumour cell lysis, which can lead to the release of high-mobility group box-1 and histones and off-target effects of CAR-T cells, resulting in hepatocyte injury. This injury affects the production of coagulation factors and exacerbates coagulation dysfunction.

According to a Chinese expert consensus, CARAC patients can be diagnosed based on the presence of elevated levels of IL-6 and other cytokines, alongside clinical manifestations of bleeding or thrombosis and abnormal coagulation indicators [16]. Typically, CARAC occurs following the onset of CRS and gradually resolves with the management of CRS [11]. Early diagnosis, accurate evaluation, and graded management based on the severity of CRS represent the cornerstone strategies for CARAC (Table 4) [16]. CRS and ICANS are graded according to the widely acknowledged American Society for Transplantation and Cellular Therapy criteria, which assess severity based on clinical features such as fever, hypotension, and hypoxia for CRS, and neurological symptoms for ICANS [97]. The anti–IL-6 receptor monoclonal antibody tocilizumab has been approved by the FDA for the treatment of severe or life-threatening CRS [98]. Current evidence indicates that tocilizumab does not significantly affect CAR-T cell expansion, antitumor efficacy, response rates, or survival outcomes [99]. Prophylactic or early administration of tocilizumab within 12 h after the onset of fever can reduce the severity and duration of CRS [100, 101]. This early intervention may help mitigate endothelial injury and thereby lowering the risk of CARAC. However, there is currently no direct evidence supporting this protective effect. Notably, prophylactic administration of tocilizumab has been implicated in the potential exacerbation of neurotoxicity [102]. However, whether tocilizumab use during established CRS increases the risk of neurotoxicity remains inconclusive. Thus, the prophylactic use of tocilizumab should be approached with caution and individualized based on patient risk factors. For patients with tocilizumab -refractory CRS, glucocorticoids are recommended. These should be initiated at an appropriate dose, titrated upward based on clinical response, and tapered gradually following symptom resolution [99]. Regular monitoring of platelet count and fibrinogen levels is essential, with the administration of platelet suspensions, fibrinogen, or cryoprecipitate necessary [16, 92]. Anticoagulant or antifibrinolytic therapy may be considered based on the individual patient’s condition [16]. The prognosis for most CARAC patients is generally favourable. In a retrospective study by Wang et al., 78.6% of patients requiring treatment recovered after cryoprecipitation, treatment with a prothrombin complex, or fibrinogen supplementation [37].

sec.title: BsAb-associated hemostatic abnormalities
sec.p: The frequency of BsAb-associated hemostatic abnormalities is lower than that of CARAC, with the former encompassing manifestations such as bleeding, thrombosis, and DIC. In a global phase III trial of patients with refractory epidermal growth factor receptor-mutant advanced NSCLC, Grade 3 or 4 bleeding events were observed in 1% of patients treated with amivantamab–chemotherapy (n = 130) and 3% with amivantamab–lazertinib–chemotherapy (n = 263) [39]. Compared with chemotherapy (n = 243), the application of amivantamab–chemotherapy and amivantamab–lazertinib–chemotherapy increased the incidence of VTE (10%, 22% vs. 5%) [39]. Moreover, in a multicentre phase II clinical trial, DIC was reported in 2% (4/189) of B-ALL patients treated with blinatumomab, and two patients experienced fatal haemorrhagic events [42]. Comprehensive research on the pathogenesis and management of BsAb-associated hemostatic abnormalities is lacking, and these abnormalities may resemble those observed with ICIs.

sec.title: Current issues and challenges
sec.p: Currently, epidemiological studies on hemostatic abnormalities associated with ICIs and BsAbs are primarily limited to retrospective analyses and case reports. These studies are inherently subject to reporting and selection biases, and their findings require validation in large-scale, prospective cohort studies. Furthermore, the heterogeneity in definitions, diagnostic criteria and populations across studies poses challenges in comparing outcomes and drawing robust conclusions. Given the potentially life-threatening nature of immunotherapy-associated hemostatic abnormalities, future efforts should emphasize standardized data collection and prospective monitoring within clinical trials to enable more accurate characterization and guide evidence-based management.

Although the pathophysiological mechanisms remain incompletely elucidated, immune-mediated inflammation and its crosstalk with coagulation are believed to be major contributors to immunotherapy-associated hemostatic abnormalities. During immunotherapy, particularly CAR-T therapy, robust immune activation induces a systemic hyperinflammatory state characterized by a cytokine storm [14, 23, 99]. Proinflammatory cytokines, such as IL-1β, IL-6, and tumor necrosis factor-α, not only amplify immune cell activation but also promote endothelial expression of procoagulant molecules (e.g., TF, P-selectin); the disruption of endothelial barrier reduces its anticoagulant properties and increases levels of antifibrinolytic mediators (e.g., plasminogen activator inhibitor-1), contributing to a hypercoagulable state [103]. In addition, immune activation promotes the release of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), which serve as scaffolds for immunothrombosis by enhancing platelet activation and local thrombus formation [104]. Massive tumor cell apoptosis or necrosis induced by immunotherapy also leads to the release of damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), such as high-mobility group box 1, ATP, histones, and cell-free DNA. These DAMPs activate pattern recognition receptors including Toll-like receptors and the NOD-like receptor protein 3 inflammasome, amplifying innate immune responses and propagating inflammatory cascades [105]. Moreover, DAMPs aggravate hemostatic dysregulation and immunothrombosis by inducing TF expression, promoting NETs formation, and compromising endothelial integrity [106]. Notably, the coagulation system exerts reciprocal regulation of immune responses through thrombin-mediated protease-activated receptor signaling and endothelial activation, exemplifying the paradigm of “immuno-coagulation coupling” [107]. These mechanisms play a pivotal role in the development of hemostatic abnormalities, forming a positive feedback loop of “tumor clearance–DAMP release–inflammation amplification–coagulation activation.” Dynamic coagulation monitoring and targeted intervention are essential for the management of high-risk patients.

Nevertheless, significant gaps persist in experimental modeling and clinical management. At present, there is a lack of clinically relevant in vitro and in vivo models that accurately recapitulate the onset and progression of these complications, limiting mechanistic exploration and the development of targeted interventions. From a clinical standpoint, key questions—such as the optimal timing for discontinuing ICIs or BsAbs upon the emergence of hemostatic abnormalities, and the safety of resuming immunotherapy after recovery—remain unanswered and warrant systematic investigation.

The primary treatment for ICI-associated ITP, Evans syndrome, iTTP, and AHA remains immunosuppression, particularly with corticosteroids. However, the potential impact of immunosuppressive therapy on the antitumor efficacy of ICIs remains controversial. A meta-analysis by Petrelli et al. demonstrated a 34% higher risk of disease progression or death in solid tumor patients who received corticosteroids during ICI therapy, regardless of the indication. Importantly, subgroup analyses revealed that corticosteroid use specifically for irAEs did not significantly affect overall survival or clinical outcomes [108]. These findings have been corroborated by large-scale clinical trial data in melanoma (ECOG-ACRIN E1609) and retrospective studies in NSCLC cohorts [109–111]. Nonetheless, these studies lacked detailed analyses of corticosteroid dosage and timing. An international multicenter retrospective study involving a large cohort of patients receiving immunosuppression for irAEs reported that higher peak corticosteroid doses (80 or 160 mg vs. 40 mg) and second-line immunosuppressants were both associated with inferior progression-free survival and overall survival, whereas cumulative corticosteroid dose did not show a significant association with survival [112]. Furthermore, in patients receiving combination anti–PD-1 and anti–CTLA-4 therapy, early initiation of immunosuppression was more strongly associated with poorer survival outcomes, suggesting that the detrimental impact of immunosuppression may be closely linked to the timing of intervention [112]. Careful consideration of the indication, timing, and intensity of corticosteroid use is essential in clinical decision-making.

With the emergence of novel immunotherapeutic agents and the increasing application of combination strategies involving ICIs, concerns have arisen regarding a potential increase in the incidence and severity of hemostatic abnormalities. Such risks have been observed in regimens combining CTLA-4 and PD-1 inhibitors [28, 57]. To enhance antitumor efficacy while minimizing irAEs, new combination approaches are under active investigation in numerous clinical trials [113]. Among these, the combination of PD-1 inhibitors with CAR-T cell therapy has shown encouraging antitumor activity. PD-1 blockade prevents CAR-T cell exhaustion in the tumor microenvironment and enhances T-cell function and cytotoxicity. It also promotes sustained interferon-γ production, maintaining a pro-inflammatory tumor milieu [113]. Preclinical studies suggest that this combination does not adversely affect peripheral blood cells, including platelets [114]. In addition, a small phase I trial evaluating CAR-T therapy with pembrolizumab reported a favorable safety profile, although one grade 3 thromboembolic event was observed [115]. Further large-scale clinical studies are warranted to fully elucidate the safety of these combination strategies and their potential impact on the hemostatic system—an area that remains a critical priority for future research.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Immunotherapy has transformed cancer treatment, yet its widespread application has led to an increase in hemostatic abnormalities. These complications are linked to immune activation triggered by immunotherapy and complex interactions among activated immune cells, proinflammatory cytokines, and the coagulation‒fibrinolysis system. Further researches are needed for a comprehensive understanding. In addition to the CARAC expert consensus, standard treatments for primary coagulopathies such as ITP, Evans syndrome, iTTP, AHA, thrombosis, and DIC are recommended. Considering the potential for these conditions to be life-threatening, vigilant monitoring and multidisciplinary collaborative management are essential for early identification and intervention.
